item.title: How NOT to be agentic
item.description: Why being afraid of failure is the antithesis of developing agency.
item.content:encoded:
As far as I can remember, I have always been afraid of taking chances. I would say that I’m a naturally risk-averse person. From the outside world, this hasn’t had much of an effect on my life. I’ve been fairly successful in all of the things I’ve tried and all of the things that people generally care about. School, career, hobbies/skills, etc. I seem to know what I’m doing and have results to show for it.

However, something that’s become more popular recently, and therefore brought to my attention, is this idea of agency. People can do things they want, regardless of their background, level of experience, or some other trait that you’d generally tie to success. I’m sure this idea/concept is something that has existed for a long time, and maybe you’ve known about it for a lot longer than I have, but this is something I’ve felt I’ve been missing for as long as I can remember, without really being able to articulate what it is that I’m missing.

I said earlier that I am naturally risk-averse, and I think this is at odds with my wants of being agentic. I always remember wanting to be taught how to do something, rather than just going and doing it. When I was learning how to play an instrument, I never liked guessing at notes until I was able to play a familiar tune; rather, I’d look for the sheet music or try to find someone else, who knew how to play what I wanted, to teach me. While improving my own life, I’ve looked to others for the systems that they’ve implemented and tried to mimic what they do. When looking for a college major, I chose based on what was the best option for “people like me” and something a random dude on TikTok said was a good decision. Even when playing video games, I would look for guides or people to learn from, rather than exploring or experiencing things on my own accord.

I think this phenomenon is similar to something people in the tech world refer to as “tutorial hell”. Generally, this refers to a beginner programmer who is constantly looking for tutorials on how to implement projects they want to create step-by-step. The main difference here is that I’m not looking for a tutorial on how to make a calculator in Python; I’m looking for a tutorial on how to live my life.

While this is obviously something that doesn’t exist, I have spent hundreds, if not thousands, of hours consciously (or subconsciously) looking for these tutorials in the books I read, videos I watch, reels/TikToks I scroll, classes I take, or even people I talk to. However, in this constant search for a tutorial, I am never properly grappling with the lessons this material is trying to teach. Just like the programmer stuck in tutorial hell, I watch these videos thinking I’m making progress, all the while, I am just stuck in the same spot I was when I started.

Now, what does any of this have to do with agency? If not already painfully obvious, this risk aversion or fear of failure has definitely had some negative effects on my level of agency. Agentic people are often labeled as people who “just do things”. They experiment with the world around them, try something new, either succeed or fail, and then decide to continue trying or look elsewhere. I honestly believe the main thing stopping more people from being agentic is the willingness to experiment and fail. I know that is definitely something that is stopping me.

As the title of this post suggests, I don’t have a guide for you on how to be agentic; furthermore, I don’t think there is anyone in the world with a guide for YOU specifically to be agentic. And if you continue looking for one, you’re going to get caught in the same cycle that I’ve been in for the past few years. If there’s one thing I suggest NOT to do it’s to look for this type of guide. And if my experience doesn’t resonate with you, then perhaps you already have agency, or your lack of it stems from something completely different.

Although, for me personally, I’m going to try being more genuinely curious and grapple with the fact that failure is a part of the process of becoming “agentic”. I also think that re-framing curiosity to childlike wonder might make things click more. While writing this, I’ve been trying to think of examples where I wasn’t afraid of failure, and they all happen to be when I was young enough to not even realize I was failing. Whether or not a truly agentic person has to work towards obtaining agency is unknown to me, but I’d like to find out myself without looking for someone else’s answer.

P.S. I haven’t written for others to read in a long time and don’t really know how people format things on Substack, but I thought that looking up “how to write on Substack” would be completely against everything I just wrote, so I hope anyone reading this enjoyed it!
